note_prices: Land prices exist in no EO catalog; VIIRS nightlights paywalled Jun 2026. All land-value links below are PROXIES via construction or population.

questions.title: Can drift see a whole-cell flip, when it was blind to a 1% one?
questions.why: Forest loss failed at 0.25 km² out of 25. A reservoir drawing down or refilling flips up to the entire 25 km² cell. If drift is a real change detector with a resolution floor, this is where it should finally fire.
questions.expected: Reservoir cells should couple to rainfall swings far more strongly than matched cropland — we predicted a clear separation, AUC well above 0.60.
questions.method: 862 inland water cells (WorldCover >50% water) paired with cropland cells in the same state. Per cell, Spearman across 2018–24 between corrected drift and |year-on-year rain-anomaly swing|. Three independent sources: water mask = WorldCover, driver = CHIRPS, signal = AlphaEarth.
questions.got:
No separation at all — AUC 0.493. Reservoir cells couple to rainfall swings at ρ +0.321; matched cropland at ρ +0.357. The farmland is if anything more rain-coupled than the water. A whole-cell flip does not rescue drift.

But the test found something we were not looking for: both groups sit far above a shuffled-year null of +0.000. Drift genuinely does track year-on-year rainfall volatility — everywhere, not just on water. That is a real positive, and it is the first one.

questions.title: Does the ground visibly change where buildings go up?
questions.why: An early signal of development is exactly what a land-value model wants — land prices are in no satellite catalog, so construction is the closest open proxy.
questions.expected: Construction is permanent and high-contrast, so we predicted drift should detect it far better than it detected forest loss — AUC around 0.65–0.75.
questions.method: GHS-BUILT-S growth as the event, cells paired on state and 2015 built-up level. Tested concurrently and as a true lead, against a trivial baseline that just extrapolates past growth. NOTE: the 2025 GHSL epoch is MODELLED, not observed.
questions.got:
Drift does not merely fail — it runs backwards. AUC 0.449, 95% CI [0.442, 0.456], excluding 0.50. Cells that gained buildings drift less than cells that did not: construction converts a churning farm surface into a static one, exactly as the noise-floor ordering predicted.

And the trivial baseline that uses no satellite data at all — where it grew in 2010–15, it grows again — scores 0.977. The embedding adds nothing over knowing the past.

questions.title: Is India's built-up growth sprawl or infill — and where are the people?
questions.why: Infill and sprawl push land value in opposite geographies: infill lifts the core, sprawl lifts the fringe. This question uses NO drift, so nothing the referee killed can touch it.
questions.expected: We expected the classic developing-country pattern: growth dominated by expansion into rural cells, with infill a minor share.
questions.method: GHS-BUILT-S 1990→2020, observed epochs only. Each epoch's built-up GAIN is attributed to the stratum the cell started in: core, fringe, or rural. Then per state, infill share against WorldPop density.
questions.got:
Neither sprawl nor infill — the fringe. Cells that were already 0.5–5% built took 60.2% of all new construction in 1990–2000 and 74.6% by 2015–2020. Over the same 30 years the core's share collapsed 16.7% → 7.7% and virgin rural fell to 17.7%.

India is not building new towns and is not densifying its cores. It is thickening the ring that was already half-built — and doing so more single-mindedly every decade. This is the one question here that uses no drift at all, so nothing the referee killed can touch it.

questions.title: Is the peri-urban conversion frontier India's highest-change land?
questions.why: The rural→suburban step is where land value multiplies hardest. If the embedding marks that frontier, it maps conversion without any price data.
questions.expected: Cells crossing rural→suburban should carry clearly the highest corrected change in the country — we predicted a visible step above every other group.
questions.method: GHS-SMOD class at 2015 vs 2020. Corrected drift and novelty averaged 2018–20 per transition group (MEDIAN — corrected drift is MAD-standardised and right-skewed, so group means compare skew, not level); plus a matched test (5241 pairs, same state AND same land cover) of converting vs staying rural.
questions.got:
Inverted, again. Cells converting rural→suburban sit at -0.214 corrected drift while cells that stayed rural sit at +0.170. Matched on state and land cover, AUC 0.418, CI [0.411, 0.427] — excluding 0.50.

By this measure the conversion frontier is the calmest land in the country, not the most active. Same mechanism as Q4: urbanisation stabilises a surface that farming keeps churning.

questions.title: Do people arrive where the land changed, or does land change where people are?
questions.why: Population inflow is the demand side of land price. The direction of the arrow decides whether land change is a leading or a trailing indicator.
questions.expected: We expected a weak but detectable positive arrow in at least one direction, most likely land-changes-first.
questions.method: WorldPop 2017 vs 2020 against corrected drift, Spearman on 113,956 cells with >10 people/km². THIN BY CONSTRUCTION: free WorldPop stops at 2020, so this is a 3-year population window against 8 years of embeddings.
questions.got:
As a straight arrow, dead in both directions — ρ -0.065 land-first, ρ -0.011 people-first. But the deciles are a U.

Cells losing population fastest sit at +0.540 corrected drift and cells gaining fastest at +0.531, while demographically stable cells bottom out at +0.216. Extremes against the middle scores AUC 0.550, CI [0.546, 0.554]. Land change marks demographic instability in either direction — which is precisely why the linear correlation reads zero. The naive test would have called this nothing.

verdict_html:
One sentence for all five. Corrected drift measures surface volatility, not development — it tracks rainfall swings everywhere (ρ≈0.33 against a 0.00 null), runs backwards on construction and on urban conversion because building stabilises land that farming churns, and is U-shaped in population because both collapse and boom disturb the ground while stability does not.

What that costs us. For the land-value question this grid is the wrong instrument: a baseline that ignores satellites entirely predicts where India builds at AUC 0.977, against 0.63 for the embedding at its inverted best. The honest use of drift is as a disturbance detector, not a development detector.

What survived. Two things. The rainfall-volatility coupling — real, national, and the first referee-passing positive in this notebook. And Q5, which needed no embeddings at all: three-quarters of all Indian construction now lands in the already-half-built fringe. The question that ignored the fancy signal is the one that answered cleanly.
